problem: Wheelchair and wheelchair-mounted robotic arm (WMRA) control are studied separately, and no simulator or dataset supports integrated navigation+manipulation learning for wheelchair-arm systems. Existing simulators (Habitat, iGibson, RCareWorld) lack synchronized multimodal data for WheelArm-style joint policy learning.
motivation: Users of assistive robots face cognitive overhead from mode switching between wheelchair and arm; data-driven VLA-style unified control needs data, but real-world collection is costly and unsafe. A physics-based simulator would let researchers without a physical WheelArm produce training data.
key_idea: Build WheelArm-Sim in Isaac Sim (Kinova Gen3 arm on Whill CR2 wheelchair in a home) with a ROS2 human-in-the-loop teleoperation pipeline to collect a synchronized multimodal navigation+manipulation dataset.
insight: An LSTM baseline trained on the mustard-picking task captures simple trends (wheelchair navigation, gripper closure) but is weaker on end-effector details and timing, indicating the data is usable for learning but small. The paper's evidence is qualitative and there are no ablations or comparisons.
method: Simulation scenario: Isaac Sim living room with four task areas (kitchen table, coffee table, drawer workstation, shelf), built-in, custom CAD (Onshape) and online objects, including a deformable teddy bear.
WheelArm model: Kinova Gen3 arm on Whill CR2 wheelchair; arm controlled by screw-theory Newton-Raphson IK, wheelchair by ROS2 differential-drive Action Graph.

Teleoperation workflow: keyboard nodes (arm target step 0.025 m / 0.05 rad, gripper, wheelchair twist) plus an Isaac Sim GUI extension for naming files, entering instructions and start/stop; data saved to HDF5.
Data processing: asynchronous streams (pose, IMU, joint states) are linearly interpolated to RGB image timestamps.
Dataset: 13 tasks, 232 trajectories, 67,783 samples with instructions, RGB-D from wrist and wheelchair cameras, IMU, joint states, Cartesian poses and velocities.

Baseline: LSTM (hidden 128) fusing ResNet18 RGB, small depth CNN, Word2Vec instruction, joint-state and timestamp encoders through an MLP to predict next-step poses of arm, wheelchair and gripper joints (MSE loss).

setting.backbone: LSTM with ResNet18 (pre-trained) + depth CNN + Word2Vec (fine-tuned), trained on simulator data
setting.training_data: WheelArm-Sim mustard-picking task: 24 experiments (16 train, 4 val per text, 4 test); teleoperated simulated demonstrations
setting.observation: RGB-D from wrist camera and wheelchair-mounted camera, IMU, joint states, language instruction
setting.action_space: Teleoperated keyboard commands (arm end-effector pose increments, gripper, wheelchair velocity); baseline predicts next Cartesian poses and gripper joint positions

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark results; only MSE/MAE min/max ranges per output component for the mustard-picking baseline (Tables train/val), not a comparable benchmark.
results: The simulator produced a 13-task, 232-trajectory, 67,783-sample multimodal dataset. The LSTM baseline follows simple wheelchair trajectories and gripper closure but struggles with end-effector orientation and timing; the wheelchair x-position is the most error-sensitive output.
limitations: Small dataset restricts generalization and the baseline struggles on complex tasks
Keyboard teleoperation only, no human model, and no VLA baseline
